newsroom/aerix-every-part-inspection: Every-Part Inspection, Built Into the Line at Aerix
In aerospace, a missed tolerance isn't a defect, it's a recall. Aerix moved from sampled checks to inspecting every part as it's built.
Aerix machines titanium parts where a fraction of a millimeter decides whether a component flies. Their old process measured a sample and trusted the rest.
Audit requirements and the cost of a single bad part meant Aerix needed a record for every unit, not a statistical estimate of quality.
Precept integrated machine vision and measurement directly into production. Each part is checked against spec and logged the moment it is made.
First-article approvals that once took days now clear in hours, and every part ships with traceable proof it met tolerance.

newsroom/automation-should-fit-your-line: Automation Should Fit Your Line, Not Replace It
The biggest barrier to automation isn't the robots. It's the fear of tearing out a line that already works. It doesn't have to be that way.
Too many automation projects start with a rip-and-replace. That's expensive, risky, and often unnecessary.
Meet the line where it is
Most floors have years of working equipment. The goal is to add robotics that tie into what's there, not to start from zero.
Precept engineers systems around your throughput, your floor, and your parts, so automation fits the operation instead of forcing a rebuild.
Phased integration and commissioning mean the line keeps running while it gets smarter, with your team trained to run it from day one.

newsroom/axlon-two-platforms-one-line: How Axlon Brought Two Platforms Onto One Line
Axlon needed to build two vehicle platforms on a single line without losing a shift to changeover. Here's how robotic assembly made it possible.
Axlon's line was built for one platform. Adding a second meant either a costly parallel line or hours lost to manual changeover between runs. Neither fit their volume targets.
Switching tooling, fixtures, and weld paths by hand took most of a shift. Every changeover was a window where quality drifted and output stopped.
Precept engineered a robotic assembly cell with interchangeable end-of-arm tooling and stored weld programs for both platforms. Changeover became a software call, not a manual rebuild.
Two platforms now run down the same line with changeover measured in minutes. Output rose and warranty claims tied to inconsistent joints fell to near zero.
